title: Standardize: The Best Way We Know Today
subtitle: Everything you have built so far lives in your head and your hands, which means it lasts exactly as long as your memory and your energy do. Standardize is how the best way stops depending on you: you write it down. A standard is not a rule carved in stone, it is the best way you know today, held in place only until you find a better one.

hands_off_note: Chapter 23 opens Standardize, the fifth S. Chapter 22 completed Safety, the fourth S, so the home is now sorted, arranged, clean, and safe, and four of the six S's are done, but almost all of that lives in exactly one place, the person who runs the home: they know the best way to load the dishwasher, the order of the bedtime routine, the trick that keeps mornings calm, and none of it was written down. So the home works beautifully right up until the day that person is sick, away, or tired, and then it quietly stops. That is the gap the fifth S closes. Chapter 23 delivers the CONCEPT of a standard and one written standard. It teaches that things drift back not from carelessness but because a way that lives only in one head is invisible to everyone else, so everyone else does it their own way and the best way is a secret (prevent reversion, carried by the drift reframe). It delivers the hero: a standard is a recipe, the best way you know today, written down plainly so it turns out right for anyone, even on a tired day, a gift and not bureaucracy (carried by the recipe reframe and the definition box). It walks the reader through writing one plain standard for a recurring task in a few steps and putting it where the work happens, with the shortcut of asking the person who already does it best to teach it. Because writing down the best way changes nothing in the rooms, the friction meter HOLDS exactly where Safety left it and does NOT move; but for the first time a new element appears behind the needle, a catch, a ratchet, holding it against the pull back toward friction, the first thing that blocks the backslide every earlier gain could quietly suffer (a sorted room re-clutters, a clean surface re-soils, a habit lapses). audience: Readers who have finished four of the six S's and now have a home that is cleared (Sort), arranged (Straighten), kept clean and read (Shine), and made safe (Safety, Chapters 20 to 22). They sense, correctly, that almost all of what they have built lives in one person's head and hands, so it lasts only as long as that person's memory and energy and quietly drifts back the day they are tired, sick, or away. Busy home keepers and parents. They do not need Sort, Straighten, Shine, or Safety re-taught; they need to make the best way stop depending on them, without turning a warm home into an office full of rules. A home whose good ways live only in one person's head is the normal case, not a failing; a standard is a gift to the household, not a compliance demand.

Understand why the gains drift back when they live only in one head (a way that lives in one head is invisible, so everyone does it their own way and the best way is a secret; prevent reversion). Learn what a standard actually is: the best way you know today, written down, a recipe and not a rule, written plainly so it turns out right for anyone, even on a tired day. Keep a standard living by the word today, rewriting it without ceremony the moment someone finds a better way, so it is a starting point and not a cage. Write your first standard for a recurring task in a few plain steps and put it where the work happens, with the shortcut of asking the person who does it best to teach it. A standard is the best way you know today, written down, and it is how the gains last.

worked_example.space: One ordinary recurring home task, captured as a single standard card. Pick something small that mostly works only when you do it (loading the dishwasher, the morning launch-pad routine, taking out the recycling), not the hardest thing in the home but the opposite. Instead of inventing a best way, capture the one you already use: watch yourself do the task once and write the steps as you go, in plain words, as few as will do the job (most home tasks are three to six steps; if you reach step eleven you are describing your personal quirks, not the task). The card is drawn like a recipe card you would actually tape up: a plain title (for example Loading the Dishwasher), four or five short numbered steps (for example: scrape do not rinse; big items along the sides and back; bowls and cups angled down on the top rack; knives point down; run it when it is full, not before), and one line at the bottom saying where it lives (for example: inside the cabinet above the dishwasher). Then put the standard where the task happens, not in a folder somewhere sensible, so the next person meets it at the moment they need it. A perfect document nobody opens is worth less than three scrappy lines stuck in the right spot. And the shortcut: if someone in the home already does a task better than everyone else, do not invent a standard from scratch, ask them to show you and write down what they do, because the best way usually already exists, fully formed, in somebody's hands.

the_concept_and_the_rule.why_things_drift_back: The problem the fifth S answers. Everything you have built lives in your head and your hands, which means it lasts exactly as long as your memory and your energy do; a standard is how a good way of doing something stops depending on you (the drift reframe, frozen). Things drift back not because anyone is lazy or careless but because a way that lives only in one person's head is invisible to everyone else, so everyone else does it their own way, and their own way is rarely the way you worked out; multiply that by every task and every person, and the drift is not a moral failing, it is just what happens when the best way is a secret. The people who first named these steps, on the factory floors of Toyota, gave this S a blunt job: prevent reversion back to the old way, not through willpower or nagging but by making the good way visible and shared, so following it is the easy, obvious thing. A standard is how you make the best way visible.
the_concept_and_the_rule.a_standard_is_a_recipe: The hero. The word standard sounds cold, like rules, clipboards, and someone checking whether you complied, but a home standard is warmer and simpler. The recipe reframe, frozen: a standard is not bureaucracy, it is a recipe, the best way you know to make something turn out right, written down so it turns out right every time, for anyone, even on a tired day. A recipe is not a rule anyone is enforcing; it is a gift, someone worked out how to make the thing turn out well and wrote it down so you do not have to work it out from scratch, and it takes skill that lived in one person's hands and makes it available to anyone who can read. The definition of a standard, frozen: a standard is the current best way to do a recurring task, written down plainly enough that anyone in the home can follow it and get the same result, and kept open enough that it is rewritten the moment a better way is found. It does not ask for length, formality, or completeness; a good home standard is usually a few lines about one task, and the test is never how thorough it looks, it is whether the next person actually follows it and gets the result you would have gotten.
the_concept_and_the_rule.the_best_way_we_know_today: The living-standard heart. The most important word in the title is today, because it keeps a standard from becoming the very cage people fear. The today reframe, frozen: the word in the title doing the quiet work is today; a standard is not the last word, it is the current best word, and the moment someone finds a better way, the standard is not broken, it is simply what you improve. This dissolves the healthy objection to standardizing anything at home, the fear of locking the household into one rigid way forever; a standard is the opposite of that, a starting point, not a finish line. It captures the best way you know as of today so you are not forever reinventing it, and it stays fully open to being replaced; when your teenager finds a faster way to fold the laundry, the better way wins and you spend thirty seconds updating the card. Held that way, a standard is not a constraint on improvement, it is the thing that makes improvement stick: without a written standard a good new idea gets used once and forgotten, with one the improvement is captured and the next person starts from there. The living-standard line, frozen: a standard is not a rule carved in stone, it is the best way you have found so far, held in place only until you find a better one, and then rewritten without ceremony.
the_concept_and_the_rule.the_rule: The rule, frozen (hero): a standard is the best way you know today, written down. That is all a standard is, and it is how the gains last: it takes the good you have built out of your head and your hands and puts it somewhere it can hold without you, be followed by anyone, and be improved by everyone.

worked_example.applied_pass: Enough concept: making one is much smaller than it sounds, and doing one is the fastest way to feel how light a standard is. Pick a single recurring task that mostly works only when you do it, something small and ordinary you have quietly become the keeper of. Instead of inventing a best way, capture the one you already use: watch yourself do the task once and write the steps as you go, in plain words, as few as will do the job. Most home tasks come down to three to six steps; if you find yourself writing step eleven, you are describing your personal quirks, not the task, so cut back to the handful of steps that actually matter to the result. Then, the part people skip, put the standard where the task happens, not in a folder somewhere sensible; a dishwasher standard lives taped inside the cabinet above the dishwasher, because the whole value of a standard is that the next person meets it at the moment they need it. And there is a lovely shortcut: if someone in the home already does a task better than everyone else, ask them to show you and write down what they do, because the best way usually already exists, fully formed, in somebody's hands, and a standard is often just the act of making one person's good habit into everyone's.
worked_example.tally: Go and look at the friction meter, and this time notice what it does not do: it does not move. That is not a disappointment, it is the whole point of this S showing up honestly on the dial. Every chapter until now, the needle traveled because the home changed; this chapter changed nothing in the rooms, you wrote down a way of doing something you were already doing, nothing was cleared, so the needle holds exactly where Safety left it, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. But look closer, because for the first time the dial shows something new, behind the needle rather than ahead of it. Until now, every gain the needle recorded was quietly reversible: a sorted room can re-clutter, a clean surface re-soils, a good habit lapses. Standardize is the first S whose job is not to move the needle forward but to keep it from sliding back, so a small catch appears behind the needle, a ratchet holding it against the pull toward friction, and the backslide that used to be always possible is, for the first time, blocked. The needle did not advance today; it got something arguably more valuable, it stopped being able to retreat. The goal is still ahead on the calm side, because Standardize has only begun and Sustain still follows, and holding a gain in place is exactly the work these last two S's exist to do. This is a HOLD with a new anti-backslide motif, NOT a move and NOT a milestone.

callouts.quick_win: Pick one recurring thing that only really works when you do it, loading the dishwasher, the bedtime routine, taking out the recycling, and write down the best way in five plain steps. Stick it where the task happens. One standard, today.
callouts.family_challenge: Ask the person who does a task best to teach it to everyone else, and write down what they do. The best way usually already lives in someone's hands; a standard just makes it everyone's.
callouts.sixs_tip: Write the standard where the work happens, not in a binder. A note taped inside the cupboard door beats a perfect document nobody opens. The best standard is the one you cannot avoid seeing.
callouts.common_mistake: Writing a standard as a strict rule and then defending it forever. A standard you are not allowed to change becomes a cage, and people quietly route around a cage. Keep it the best way for now, and let anyone propose a better one.
